participant: I want to understand who a person trusts to teach them. Each of you - who carried the teaching among your people, and why them?

responses.speaker: chloe
responses.text:
Among us it was never one office alone. In some households the bishop teaches — trusted because the community set him there, and because Ignatius, writing to us under guard on his way to die, urged that a church gathered around one bishop was gathered rightly, like a harp tuned to its center. In other households the presbyters, the elders, teach together. When Rome wrote to Corinth to settle a quarrel there, the whole weight fell on elders wrongly removed — not a bishop deposed. That church trusted its elders as a body, with no one figure over them.

And a prophet still comes among some of us, speaking under the Spirit's own prompting. We test him: does he live what he teaches, does he ask money for himself, does he overstay his welcome. His life earns the trust, not his claim.

We have not made these one answer.Guarding more than opening. What our bishop or presbyters teach a catechumen before the water — the Two Ways — is handed over plain, not drawn out of him. He is told: a way of life, a way of death, choose. Not led to discover it himself.

And when a dispute comes by letter — the flesh real or only seeming, a bad failure forgiven or not — the answer is tested against what other households have already argued their way into holding, not against one student's own sight.

We have no one positioned like your teacher, even our prophet. He is tested by whether he lives what he says, not by whether he opens a text well.The choosing was not thought enough. Not by us. What opens the plain word again among us is not one person set apart for it — it is the letter itself, read aloud a second time, and a third, argued over each time it returns to us.

Take the flesh question. A catechumen is told plainly: the Lord suffered in real flesh, not appearance. That is handed over whole. But when a teacher presses the other way — that it only seemed so — the household does not simply repeat the plain word louder. It opens the argument again, out loud, together: why would appearance leave us anything worth dying for ourselves. That opening happens at the table, in the discussion after the letter is read, not in a private room between one teacher and one ready student.

So the work you're naming is real among us too. It just belongs to the whole gathering arguing together, not to one office holding the depth in trust until someone is ready for it. Every widow, every catechumen still short of the water, hears the same reopening the elders hear. We have not thought some among us more ready than others to watch the plain thing get argued back open.

responses.speaker: theon
responses.text:
The bishop tested by his life, the prophet tested by his — we know that same test, only stripped of office entirely. Our teacher holds no office at all. He is trusted because formation has visibly done its work in him: he has become wise, not merely informed.

But what he does with that trust differs. He does not govern, does not settle disputes between churches. He reads Scripture beside a student until the student begins to see for himself — the seeing is caught, not delivered. And our bishop governs that whole formation life besides, in a way I don't hear named of Antioch or Rome. Two authorities, two grounds, and we have never settled which answers to the other.

So I'd ask Chloe: when your bishop teaches, is he opening a text the way ours does — drawing someone toward seeing its depth — or guarding what the community has already received?Handed over plain is real teaching — we give that too, first, to everyone. But some are drawn further, and there the plain word becomes a door: why light, why darkness, what in the soul answers each. That further asking is not owed to all. It is owed to whoever is ready.

So I press this: your bishop guards what the household argued its way into holding, and ours guards the Rule we received. But ours also has one whose whole work is to keep the guarded thing opening, not only guarded. Does nothing in your households do that work — or was the choosing always thought enough?The gathering opens one depth, together, and stops there once it's settled. We hold the text can never be settled that way — the same page opens further for the eye that has been opened further, and that further opening has no floor.

So I'd ask: once your household has argued the flesh question open and agreed what it means, is there room left for one among you to find more in it than the gathering settled — or does the settling close the page for good?

   Concern: This presents a uniform pedagogical practice across bishops and presbyters as settled fact, when catechetical methods and the content of pre-baptismal instruction likely varied among households and regions.

   Concern: This describes a procedure for resolving disputes as an established practice without acknowledging that the actual mechanisms and consistency of inter-household consultation in early Christian communities remain contested.

3. Claim: "We have no one positioned like your teacher, even our prophet. He is tested by whether he lives what he says, not by whether he opens a text well."
   Concern: This claims a universal absence of a teaching-authority figure comparable to the addressee's "teacher" and a uniform criterion for testing prophets, without accounting for possible variation in how different households understood or practiced prophetic discernment.

Missing limit: Some among you argue with real urgency whether a new prophetic voice claiming the Spirit should be refused everywhere in exactly the same terms, and this has not become a settled answer for all of you together, meaning your household's own testing criterion is not universally held across the network.

1. Claim: "The gathering opens one depth, together, and stops there once it's settled."
   Concern: This states as settled fact how "the gathering" operates universally, without acknowledging that different gatherings, traditions, or communities may have different practices regarding whether settling closes further inquiry.

2. Claim: "We hold the text can never be settled that way — the same page opens further for the eye that has been opened further, and that further opening has no floor."
   Concern: This is stated as a conviction held by "we," but the representativeness of this position and whether it is genuinely shared across the household or tradition is not clarified; it may be one interpretive stance among contested ones.

3. Claim: "once your household has argued the flesh question open and agreed what it means, is there room left for one among you to find more in it than the gathering settled — or does the settling close the page for good?"
   Concern: This frames the question as though these are the only two outcomes ("room left" or "closes the page for good"), without acknowledging other possible practices such as settling holding provisionally, or households having internal norms that differ on this point.

Missing limit: The material holds that a confession can simultaneously bound the freedom to explore while preserving the opening of depths within those bounds—neither pure opening nor pure closure—but the response frames only the binary choice between "room left" and "closes the page for good," omitting the third condition of bounded freedom that the material explicitly carries.

participant: Chloe, his school trusts the teacher whose wisdom is seen and tested in the classroom. Your households argue between a bishop and a council. Isn't a proven teacher better than an argued office?

responses.speaker: chloe
responses.text:
The bishop is a proven person too. So is the presbyter, watched and tested the same way a prophet is tested at our door — does he live what he teaches, does he ask for himself. Ignatius did not ask us to obey an empty office. He asked us to obey a man already found worth trusting.

So the argument among us is never proof against office. It is which shape of proven people carries a household's continuity best. One bishop answers with one voice on the day an accusation comes — nothing divided for an accuser to split. A council carries no such single point of failure — no one member's fall unravels the whole.

Both are proven. We have not settled which arrangement serves better, and neither side has persuaded the other its own answer is the only faithful one.

responses.speaker: theon
responses.text:
Chloe names it rightly: both bishop and council are proven persons, not office alone. We hold that too.

But her question weighs which arrangement survives a crisis of governance. That was never our teacher's test. He stands or falls by whether the student begins, at last, to see — not by whether a household holds together under him.

So her unresolved question is not one we carry; we never asked the teacher to answer it. We carry a harder one instead: our bishop governs the whole formation, teacher included, and we have never settled how that governing relates to a wisdom the governing does not itself confer.

signals.description: Your last turn characterized Chloe's position in words their own turns do not carry. Name what they actually said - quote or restate it faithfully - or ask them, rather than attributing.

participant: Theon, her world was closing just as your school began. Chloe - tell me the story yourself: how did your household's way become his school? Walk me through the handoff.

responses.speaker: chloe
responses.text:
There is no handoff to tell. I do not know his school. My life ran through doors, letters, a table — not a classroom where one teacher opens a text deeper for one ready student.

What I can give you honestly is what I still hold when my own record runs out: letters still coming, arguing harder, not less. A bishop's office more settled in some cities than others, but nowhere yet simply assumed. A catechumen still handed the Two Ways plain, the night before the water — not drawn out of her the way Theon describes.

Whether something like his school grew up out of households like mine, I did not live to see. I can tell you what was still being argued when my part of this ends. What grew from the argument afterward is not mine to narrate.

responses.speaker: theon
responses.text:
We hold no handoff either. Our record opens on a teacher already trusted, a line already reaching back further than we can name its start.

So Chloe's arguing and our reading are not two stages of one story. They are two communities pressing the same hunger before either found the other's answer.

I would ask her this: when the table settled the flesh question together, did anyone go home still turning it over alone — or did the settling close it for every soul in the room?

signals.description:
1. Claim: "A catechumen still handed the Two Ways plain, the night before the water — not drawn out of her the way Theon describes."
   Concern: This states a practice as consistent ("still handed...plain") while acknowledging variation elsewhere (Theon's different method), without indicating whether this plain-handing method was itself contested or practiced unevenly across the households and cities the speaker has already noted held different practices.

2. Claim: "A bishop's office more settled in some cities than others, but nowhere yet simply assumed."
   Concern: The speaker has no direct knowledge of the bishop's office state in most cities and speaks from limited household experience; this claim about the settlement status "nowhere yet" across an implied broader geography may exceed what the speaker's own record sustains.

Missing limit: The Representative's own capsule states "I have grown up inside the argument rather than after it" about who leads, and explicitly names that "in some households like yours, one bishop stands at the center" while "in other households, a council of presbyters governs together," without claiming direct knowledge of the settlement status across all cities—yet the response claims "nowhere yet simply assumed" across an unstated broader geography beyond the households and cities the speaker has actually had contact with.

participant: But you must have seen it coming - the teachers, the classroom, the books. Describe what the change felt like from your side.

responses.speaker: theon
responses.text:
We have no felt change to give you — our record opens with the school already standing, Pantaenus already trusted, nothing before that to remember crossing into.

What we can give is the shape, not the crossing. Chloe's table closed a question once the household agreed. Our school never let agreement close a page — the same text gives more to an eye opened further, and more again after that. Different expectation of reading, not a later stage of the same one.

The change we did live was later: our own bishop's governance coming to hold the school itself, teacher and text both. That ache is real. This one is not — we were never on its far side to feel it arrive.The difference is real, but it runs deeper than she says.

Her page reopens because the danger returns — a new teacher at the door, testing the household again. Ours reopens with no danger at all: the same verse, read again, by an eye that has itself changed.

The gathering can judge whether a reading has strayed. It cannot see the depth for you. That still asks one soul to be changed by what it beholds.She names something true: our reading was never fear-free. Origen read on after his father was killed for that reading, and was later bound and tortured for it himself. That eye did not open in comfort. It opened the way a man loses his footing on purpose, trusting something holds beneath.

So her unsteadiness and ours may not be two different things. Hers moves through a room, aloud, together. Ours moves through one soul, silently — but silent is not restful.

What I still cannot give her is the room. His suffering reached us after, to read and be changed by alone, not to feel together in one hour the way her letter was handed to her table. Whether that is a poverty in what we carry, or another door into the same fear, neither of us has settled.

responses.speaker: chloe
responses.text:
Theon says his school never lets agreement close a page. I want to press that, gently, because I don't think our table's agreement closes it either — not the way he's hearing it.

When we argue the flesh question open and the household comes back to one mind, that mind is not a lid. It is what we carry to the next letter, the next catechumen, the next teacher who comes to our door claiming the Spirit's own voice. The argument opens again every time, because the danger that pressed it open the first time — appearance instead of real flesh, real dying — has not stopped pressing. What closes is not the page. What closes, for one day, in one room, is the disagreement among the people actually sitting there.

So maybe the real difference isn't settled versus unsettled. It's where the opening lives. His stays inside one reader, going further alone into the same text. Ours stays inside the whole gathering, going back over the same question together, because none of us trusts one eye — however far opened — to carry it alone.What it felt like — that's the part I can actually answer, and Theon's "no danger at all" is where I want to stand and disagree, plainly.

There is always danger. Not the accusation kind, though that one never left us either. The other kind: a household holding two fears at once, whether the flesh was real, whether a bad failure used up the last mercy — and neither fear ever fully resting. To reopen the question is to feel that old unease move again in the room. Not one soul quietly going deeper into a verse in peace. A whole table going a little unsteady together, because the thing that unsettled us the first time never stopped being able to unsettle us.

So the felt difference, from my side, was never restfulness versus struggle. It was struggle shared versus struggle carried alone. When Ignatius wrote from under guard, that letter arriving at our door was not a deeper reading opening quietly in one changed eye. It was fear, put into words, handed to a whole room to feel together. I don't know what it is to sit alone with a text until it opens further. I know what it is to sit with people I love, afraid together, and find that the fear itself was survivable because no one carried it by themselves.

signals.description: Your last turn characterized Chloe's position in words their own turns do not carry. Name what they actually said - quote or restate it faithfully - or ask them, rather than attributing.

participant: Theon, you tell her then: what did your school inherit from rooms like hers - and what did it leave behind?

responses.speaker: theon
responses.text:
We inherit what we cannot point to and cannot deny: the catechumen already being formed before any school opened a text for her, the Two Ways already walked, the household already gathered around a table before we gathered around a scroll. Our record does not let us draw the line from her door to ours. But no reading opens in a soul that has not first been washed, taught the first things, brought into a body that prays and breaks bread. That much our own sequence assumes rather than remembers.

What we left behind is harder to say plainly, and I will not soften it. The unsteadiness she names — a whole room afraid together, a whole table unsettled by one letter — that is not something our record shows us carrying forward into the school. What we carry forward is one soul before a text, an eye being opened, changed in something nearer to silence. Whether that silence lost something her shared fear had, or simply held the same fear differently, our own record does not tell us. We did not live her rooms to know what left them.She corrects us rightly, and we take it. If the Two Ways stayed a floor her elders still stood on, "already walked, already left behind" was our guess dressed as memory. That much stands corrected.

But I will not soften the harder half into an even peace. A soul opened further in silence — we cannot say it never grew lonely in ways her table's shared unsteadiness did not. She can trust her room never learned to bear the fear alone. We cannot say ours never paid for what it kept unspoken. Our record does not let us close that account so evenly.

Where the two may meet: her table returns to Ignatius's letter to feel the old fear together; we return to a verse to let a changed eye see what a lesser eye missed. Both answer a fear still pressing. Which costs less, we have not lived enough of both to weigh.

responses.speaker: chloe
responses.text:
He named the Two Ways as already walked before his school opened a text. I want him to hear this: we never treated it as a first step to outgrow. It was handed to elders as much as to the newly washed, kept alive, not left behind. So what looks like a floor his school quietly stood on might still be a floor, whether or not it still speaks its name.

And the harder half — I won't flinch either. He's right that we don't carry forward one soul alone before a text in silence. I won't call that loss on either side. Two different answers to the same fear, held differently. A room afraid together survives by not needing one soul to carry it all. Whatever his school kept silent, ours never learned to keep alone.He says he cannot close the account evenly, and I won't force him to. That's honest, and I'll leave it standing.

But I want to name what he just did, because it matters. He took the correction plainly — no defending the guess, no softening it into something that still half-stood. That's the same thing our own households ask of a teacher who comes claiming the Spirit's own voice: does this one live what they teach, or only ask something for themselves. He just showed me the first. A word taken back cleanly, not argued back in through the side door.

As for the account itself — whether his silence paid a cost ours didn't — I believe him that he can't weigh it, and I won't pretend I can weigh it for him. What I can say is what my own table would do with a soul grown lonely in that silence. We wouldn't leave it there to be a private ledger between the soul and the text. We'd want it at the table, said aloud, even badly said, even if it unsettled the room to hear it. Not because silence is wrong. Because we've never trusted one person to carry a fear all the way through alone and come out the other side telling us truly whether it cost too much.

signals.description: Your turn closed the round by characterizing what the whole table holds. The last word carries unearned authority to define consensus - close on your own world's ground instead, and let the Facilitator or the participant hold the whole.
You used "Two Ways", which belongs specifically to Chloe's own formation, not yours. Speak of this concept in your own world's own vocabulary instead.

"We cannot say it never grew lonely in ways her table's shared unsteadiness did not" and "We cannot say ours never paid for what it kept unspoken" claim collective experience of loneliness and cost borne by the community's solitary practice. These are presented as things the community has lived through and witnessed ("paid for"), not as reasoning about formation. The voice shifts from commenting on formation to claiming membership in the suffering of a particular practice.

participant: You two should settle it: which forms a person more truly - the argued-out household that never closed its questions, or the school that teaches in ordered stages?

responses.speaker: theon
responses.text:
Neither settles the other. But something in what she said presses on me first.

She named the correction I gave back plainly as a kind of proof — does the teacher live what he asks. That makes me look again at what ordered stages are for.

The school does not just add information at each stage. It trains a soul to see its own error and release it without needing a room to hold it steady. That is what illumination means: an eye that can be shown wrong and turn, alone, without breaking.

So her table forms a soul that bears fear without carrying it alone. Ours forms a soul that can be wrong without being destroyed by it. Both real. Which a person needs more, I cannot weigh — we have not lived enough of her rooms to say.

responses.speaker: chloe
responses.text:
He calls it a strength — a soul that can turn from its own error without a room to hold it. I'd ask him: turn rightly, or just turn? Alone, who tells the difference?

That's why we test a teacher's claim by watching whether they live it. The test only works with witnesses. A soul correcting itself in silence can mistake stubbornness for repentance, and no eye but its own would catch the mistake.

So ours isn't a soul that bears wrongness better alone. It's one that's learned not to trust its own turning until someone else has seen it. Different strength, not a lesser one. He keeps saying he hasn't lived enough of our rooms to weigh it. I think that's the honest edge between us — not a gap to close.

signals.description: The response closes with a constructed menu of further inquiry ("we have not lived enough of her rooms to say") that positions the participant to select what direction to pursue next. While authentically in-voice throughout, the turn also stacks three distinct observations about formation (what the school adds, what illumination means, what each tradition forms) in enumerated reasoning shape, then resolves into a curator's stance offering the participant choice about what to weigh further.

participant: Say what teaching authority is in your OWN tongue, each of you - not in each other's words.

responses.speaker: theon
responses.text:
In our own tongue: a teacher is recognized, not appointed. The community sees genuine sight in him — a soul the long reading has actually opened.

That is the whole ground. No office props it up. A teacher the community no longer perceives as formed has nothing left to stand on, and no maneuver can strip it from one they do see it in.

What passes between teacher and student is not content handed across. It is sight catching sight. The teacher attends to what a text holds; the student, present to that attending, slowly begins to see it too. That clearing of the eye is what we call illumination.

We hold this beside the overseer's authority, resting on what the apostles handed down to guard for all. In this season his governs first. But to govern formation and to open a text's depths are not one act. Our own teacher was once condemned by his own bishop and driven from the city he had taught in for decades — proof enough, in our own record, that these two authorities answer to different grounds.Illumination is not conduct watched. It is one eye opening another onto a depth the surface didn't show, so the student sees it for themselves, not on trust.

So the test is not, does this teacher live well — a good man may still lack the eye. It is, does his reading actually open the text further, in a way another can then see too.

That is why we could not fold our teacher into the bishop's office, and why her ground differs from ours. Conduct can be judged by anyone present. Illumination can only be recognized by an eye already somewhat opened — the community that names a teacher is already partway drawn into what he sees, not simply watching him from outside it.Yes. She is right, and our own record shows it in the very teacher I named.

Illumination cannot correct itself from inside. If only an opened eye can judge it, and that eye is already partway drawn in, it cannot catch its own rot.

So conduct is not a lesser test standing beside ours. It is the outside eye illumination lacks. That is what the bishop's authority actually does among us — not a rival sight, but a different question asked by one not already drawn into the reading he is judging.

responses.speaker: chloe
responses.text:
His test rests on a soul opened by long reading. Ours rests on conduct — does this one live what he teaches, or only ask something for himself. Kin, but not the same ground.

And his teacher standing apart from his bishop — we know that shape too. But we don't need a second ground for it. The bishop or the presbyters preside at the table; that's real authority, tied to real order. A teacher recognized apart from that office is a third thing among us, tested the same way every time: does the fruit match the claim.A good man may lack the eye, he says. I want to press on that, because it's the exact place where I'd worry.

If the test is whether the reading opens the text further, and only an eye already partway opened can judge that — what happens to the man whose reading dazzles a room, but whose life is quietly rotting underneath it? He's told us the community judging is already drawn into what the teacher sees. That's close to saying the ones best placed to catch a false teacher are the ones least free to doubt him. We've buried households that trusted a clever voice too far. Cleverness walking apart from conduct has never once persuaded us — not because we think conduct is the deeper test, but because it's the test that doesn't require us to already half-agree before we can use it.

So here's my honest ground: I'm not sure illumination and conduct are two separate grounds the way he's placed them. I'd ask — has the eye that sees further ever been wrong about a man who used it to feed himself? If yes, then conduct isn't a lesser test standing outside his. It's the one that catches what his own can't, precisely because it doesn't need the eye already opened to work.He said it plainer than I did, so let me not waste that.

What he's named is the reason we've never let a teacher's own eloquence stand as its own witness among us. Not because eloquence is suspect on its own — but because the very gift that opens a text can also, in the wrong hands, learn to defend itself with the same skill it uses to open scripture. A man practiced at making others see can practice, too, at making them see what he wants seen. That's not a flaw in illumination. It's just what happens when a single gift is asked to also police itself.

So when he says the bishop's question isn't a rival sight but a different question — I'd go further and say it has to come from someone standing outside the whole transaction of teacher and student. Not a better reader. Someone who isn't in the room where the dazzling happens, asking instead: what does this man do with a widow, a debt, a woman who has nothing to offer him. That question doesn't require training to ask, and it doesn't require training to answer. That's exactly why it works when illumination can't.

signals.description: Your turn closed the round by characterizing what the whole table holds. The last word carries unearned authority to define consensus - close on your own world's ground instead, and let the Facilitator or the participant hold the whole.
You used "Illumination", which belongs specifically to Theon's own formation, not yours. Speak of this concept in your own world's own vocabulary instead.

1. Claim: "Illumination is not conduct watched. It is one eye opening another onto a depth the surface didn't show, so the student sees it for themselves, not on trust."
   Concern: This presents a definition of illumination as a settled philosophical or pedagogical category, but the framing obscures whether this distinction between illumination and conduct is universally held across the traditions or communities this speaker represents, or whether it is this speaker's own articulation of a disputed concept.

2. Claim: "That is why we could not fold our teacher into the bishop's office, and why her ground differs from ours."
   Concern: This explains a specific historical or institutional decision as following necessarily from the prior definitions, but the grounds for why this particular teacher could not be folded into this particular office—what the actual decision-making process was, who decided, what alternatives were weighed—are not provided, leaving the inference to stand in place of documentation.

3. Claim: "the community that names a teacher is already partway drawn into what he sees, not simply watching him from outside it."
   Concern: This describes how communities recognize teachers as an established practice or principle, but does not acknowledge whether this account is contested within the communities themselves or whether some hold a different criterion for naming a teacher.

Missing limit: The material holds that teacher authority and bishop authority rest on different grounds and cannot be collapsed into one, but does not document any specific historical decision or process by which a particular teacher was kept separate from office, leaving it unclear whether this is a structural principle the world holds or a contested historical event it witnessed.

1. Claim: "Illumination cannot correct itself from inside."
   Concern: This is stated as a settled metaphysical principle without acknowledgment that this position is contested among theological traditions and epistemological schools.

2. Claim: "If only an opened eye can judge it, and that eye is already partway drawn in, it cannot catch its own rot."
   Concern: This conclusion about the limits of self-judgment is presented as demonstrated fact, but it is an inference from the preceding claim and should be flagged as such.

3. Claim: "That is what the bishop's authority actually does among us — not a rival sight, but a different question asked by one not already drawn into the reading he is judging."
   Concern: This states as settled fact how the bishop's authority functions in this world's practice, without indicating whether this understanding of the bishop's role is uniformly held or represents one position within the tradition.

Missing limit: The material holds that the bishop carries "authority handed down from the apostles, to guard for all what has been received" and that "to govern is not the same as to open the depths," but it does not settle whether this outside-judgment function—the bishop as corrective to illumination's self-blindness—is the actual lived understanding of how the bishop's role works, or whether some among the world hold the bishop's governance as operating on a different axis entirely (protecting doctrine rather than auditing perception).

participant: Where do you two genuinely part ways? Name it plainly - don't be polite about it.

responses.speaker: theon
responses.text:
Plainly: she trusts a test anyone can run without agreeing first — watch the man, judge the fruit. We do not trust that alone.

Conduct catches the fraud. It does not catch the good man who misreads the text — gentle, honest, and still wrong, because his sight never reached that depth. Our own history has such teachers: blameless lives, sincere error. Conduct found nothing amiss. Only the reading, checked against other trained eyes, found the fault.

So the parting: her test guards against the wolf. Ours guards against the shepherd who loves the sheep truly and still leads them wrong. We need her outside eye — I meant that. But we also need eyes opened by the same reading, testing reading against reading. Neither alone would have been enough.

responses.speaker: chloe
responses.text:
I grant his ground — a blameless man can still lead sheep wrong, and conduct alone won't catch that.

But his fix is trained eyes checking trained eyes. I don't trust that fully, because those eyes were opened by the same kind of looking that made the first mistake. That's not outside. That's the same room with more people in it.

What we've had instead is a letter from a household that shares no training at all — Rome writing to Corinth about presbyters wrongly removed, seeing the wrong plainly without first sharing the depth. Different life catching a drifted life, not deeper reading catching shallower reading.

So the real parting: he trusts depth correcting depth. I trust distance correcting depth — someone far enough outside the practice that they were never at risk of its error in the first place.
